source_document.body:
Zim Integrated Shipping Services reported third-quarter net income of $830 million, up from $123 million a year earlier, as sharply higher freight rates lifted revenue and prompted another increase in its full-year earnings forecast.
The Haifa, Israel-based container carrier (NYSE: ZIM ) said that revenue rose 53% to $2.71 billion in the three months ended Sept. 30. Diluted earnings per share increased to $6.88 from $1.02.
Average freight rates climbed 55% year over year to $2,480 per twenty-foot equivalent unit , or TEU, while cargo volume increased 4% to 962,000 TEUs, as pricing, rather than volume growth, provided the main lift to quarterly revenue.
Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization increased 124% to $1.33 billion. Adjusted operating earnings, or EBIT, reached $993 million, compared with $260 million a year earlier, while the adjusted EBIT margin expanded to 37% from 15%.
“By keeping our network agile and focusing on premium, profitable trades, we are supporting our customers and positioning ZIM for further growth,” President and Chief Executive Chen Lichtenstein said in the earnings release.
Rates remained unusually strong on both coasts, Lichtenstein said on a call with analysts, noting Asia-U.S. West Coast and East Coast market conditions had not experienced the typical late-summer decline seen in prior years. He linked the broader freight-rate strength to port congestion, particularly in China, and disruptions affecting major shipping passages.
“We do see some softening in recent weeks,” he said, attributing it to customers delaying orders and avoiding bringing products into the U.S. around Christmas and year-end. “There is an expectation that the market will pick up again in January before the Chinese New Year,” he added.
Lichtenstein said e-commerce was feeding demand for expedited trans-Pacific services, while Zim had established a task force focused on suppliers serving AI and data centers. He also identified opportunities to shift cargo from airfreight to expedited ocean shipping.
Management said freight forwarders handle much of the high-value cargo Zim targets and had paid higher average rates than direct cargo owners on both Asia-U.S. coasts in each of the past three years. Lichtenstein also emphasized limiting annual contract volumes to preserve pricing flexibility.
Zim now expects full-year adjusted EBITDA of $3.3 billion to $3.5 billion and adjusted EBIT of $2 billion to $2.2 billion. Its previous ranges were $2.7 billion to $3 billion and $1.4 billion to $1.7 billion, respectively.
The increase follows Zim’s October guidance upgrade, when it cited strong market demand and favorable freight-rate momentum.
The stronger results also echo Hapag-Lloyd’s ( HLAG.DE ) third-quarter performance, which showed higher freight rates driving a sharp profit increase despite broadly unchanged cargo volumes.
Zim’s reported earnings benefited from a non-cash reversal of an earlier asset impairment. Adjusted net income, which excludes that benefit and acquisition-related costs, totaled $717 million, up from $124 million a year earlier. The impairment reversal added $155 million after tax to reported profit, while acquisition-related costs totaled $41 million after tax.
Zim generated $1.24 billion in operating cash flow and $1.22 billion in free cash flow during the quarter. Net debt, which includes lease liabilities, fell to $1.86 billion at Sept. 30 from $2.77 billion at June 30.
The board declared a dividend of $2.01 per share, or approximately $243 million, representing about 30% of aggregate net income for the first nine months of 2026.
For the first nine months, revenue increased to $5.89 billion from $5.42 billion, while net income rose to $808 million from $443 million. Cargo volume slipped to 2.75 million TEUs from 2.765 million.
New services as takeover review continues
Zim said it launched ZX3, its third premium expedited Asia-U.S. West Coast service, and Falcon, offering faster transit times from China to Argentina and southern Brazil. The carrier currently operates 112 containerships with combined capacity of approximately 703,000 TEUs, along with 13 car carriers.
Meanwhile, Hapag-Lloyd’s proposed acquisition of Zim for $35 per share in cash remains subject to regulatory approvals, including Israel’s consent under its special state share. Zim said the original application to the Israeli government was terminated and Hapag-Lloyd intends to submit a new application soon.
FreightWaves previously reported that Israel required a new review of the takeover after objections to the original transaction structure prompted a revised proposal.
Zim now says the transaction is targeted to close in the first quarter of 2027. The carriers remain separate, independent companies until closing.
Why it matters: For shippers, the launch of another expedited Asia-U.S. West Coast service adds a premium routing option, while the upgraded outlook signals management expects a stronger full-year financial result.
